A squatter is a person who moves into and lives in a place — usually a building or a piece of land — that does not belong to them, without the owner's permission, without paying rent, and without any legal right to be there.

Think of it this way: imagine a house that has been empty and abandoned for years. Nobody lives in it, nobody is watching it. One day, a person simply walks in, sets up their belongings, and starts living there as if it were their home. That person is a squatter. They didn't buy the property. They didn't sign a lease. They didn't ask anyone. They just occupied it.

The verb behind this word is "to squat," which in this context means to settle on or occupy a place without any legal claim to it.

People become squatters for a variety of reasons, most often connected to hardship:

  • Poverty and homelessness — They cannot afford to rent or buy a place to live, so they occupy an empty building just to have shelter.
  • Lack of housing — In many cities, especially in developing countries, there is simply not enough affordable housing for everyone, so large groups of people settle on unused land and build makeshift homes.
  • Political protest — Some squatters deliberately occupy unused properties as a form of social or political protest, arguing that it is wrong for buildings to sit empty while people are homeless.
  • Seeking land — Historically, people moved onto unoccupied land (often government-owned) to farm it and build a life, hoping to claim it as their own over time.
Two Main Contexts: Modern and Historical

1. The Modern Meaning (Most Common)

Today, when people say "squatter," they almost always mean someone who is occupying an empty or abandoned property without permission. This is the universal, everyday meaning.

This could be:

  • A homeless person who moves into an abandoned house in a city.
  • A group of activists who occupy an empty commercial building to protest housing shortages.
  • A family in a developing country who builds a shack on unused land at the edge of a city because they have nowhere else to go.

2. The Historical Meaning (Australia and the American West)

The word "squatter" also has important historical meanings that are quite different in tone — and even somewhat positive.

In Australian history, squatters were wealthy pastoralists (farmers who raised sheep and cattle) who moved their livestock onto vast stretches of government-owned land in the 18th and 19th centuries without any formal permission or license to do so. Over time, many of these squatters became extremely powerful and influential — they formed the backbone of Australia's rural elite. Eventually, many of them were granted formal legal rights to the land they occupied. So in Australian history, calling someone a "squatter" carries a sense of being a pioneering, if unauthorised, landowner — not a homeless person. This historical class of people is still known as "the squattocracy" (a word combining squatter and aristocracy).

In American history, squatters were settlers who moved onto unsettled or government-owned land on the frontier, particularly in the 18th and 19th centuries, without any legal title. They would clear the land, build homes, and farm it — gambling that they would eventually be allowed to purchase it legally. Many of America's early settlements grew from squatting.

This is one of the most fascinating and important concepts connected to the word "squatter," and it is very real in law.

In many countries, if a squatter occupies a piece of land or property openly, continuously, and without the owner's objection for a long enough period of time (which varies by country and region — it could be anywhere from 5 to 20+ years), they may actually earn the legal right to own that property. This legal principle is called adverse possession, but it is commonly known as squatter's rights.

The idea behind it is practical: if a property owner completely ignores their property and never challenges someone living on it for many years, the law in many places recognises the person who has actually been using and maintaining the land as its rightful owner. The law essentially asks, "Who has been acting like the real owner all along?"

This does not happen easily or automatically. The squatter usually has to meet very strict legal conditions, and the process is complex. But it is a genuine legal concept, not a myth.

In many parts of the world — particularly in rapidly growing cities in Africa, Asia, and Latin America — large communities of squatters form together in what are called squatter settlements. These are areas, usually on the edges of cities, where people have built their own homes on land they do not own.

These settlements go by many names: slums, shantytowns, favelas (in Brazil), townships (in South Africa), or informal settlements. They often lack basic infrastructure like clean water, electricity, sewage systems, and paved roads — because, since the residents have no legal claim to the land, the government and utility companies typically do not provide services to them.

Some of the world's most famous examples include the favelas of Rio de Janeiro (Brazil), Dharavi in Mumbai (India), and Kibera in Nairobi (Kenya). Hundreds of millions of people worldwide live as squatters in such settlements.
How a Squatter Differs from Similar People

It helps to understand this word by comparing it to related terms:

  • A tenant pays rent and has a legal agreement (a lease) with the owner. A squatter pays nothing and has no agreement at all.
  • A trespasser enters a property without permission, but usually just passes through or enters briefly. A squatter actually lives in a place and treats it as their home — they stay.
  • A homeless person does not necessarily occupy a specific building or land. A squatter has specifically settled in and occupies a particular space.

The legal status of squatting varies significantly from place to place.

  • In many countries and states, squatting is a criminal offense — meaning the squatter can be arrested.
  • In other places, it is treated as a civil matter, meaning the property owner cannot have the squatter arrested but must go through a court to legally remove them (a process called eviction). This can sometimes take months or even years.
  • In some places, the law distinguishes between squatting in a residential property (one meant for people to live in) versus squatting in a commercial property (like an office or warehouse), treating these differently.

A squatter is someone who occupies property — a building, a piece of land, or any space — without owning it, paying for it, or having legal permission to be there. In modern usage, this word most often refers to a homeless or impoverished person seeking shelter, or to communities of people building homes on unused land. Historically, it referred to pioneering settlers who occupied government-owned land to farm it. The concept of "squatter's rights" (adverse possession) means that, in some cases and after a very long time, a squatter may even earn legal ownership of the property they have occupied.
